explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick that, friend, but the text says otherwise. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, took their censers, put fire in them and added incense. Then the verse says they “…offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.” So that fire was not what the LORD had commanded.

That's right, friend. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, put fire in their censers and added incense. Then the text says they “…offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.” That one phrase tells you what went wrong in verse 1.

Fire is the word. The text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed Nadab and Abihu, and they died in the presence of the LORD. Their own fire was in their censers, and this fire came from the LORD's presence. I think this is one of the heavy verses, friend.

Smoke is a reasonable guess, since incense was in those censers. But the text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them. Nadab and Abihu died in the presence of the LORD. I think this is a heavy verse.

Wind is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD. It consumed Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, and they died in the presence of the LORD. I think this one is heavy.
That's it. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron what the LORD meant, and the text says “But Aaron remained silent.” No speech and no answer, just silence. I think there's a lot packed into that quiet.

The text doesn't say that, friend. After Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron what the LORD meant, it says “But Aaron remained silent.” Aaron says nothing at all in that moment. I think that silence says plenty.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a natural guess, but it's not what the verse says. Moses, Israel's leader, explains what the LORD meant, and then we read “But Aaron remained silent.” Aaron doesn't cry out or say a single word there. Sometimes the Bible lets a quiet moment stay quiet.

Outside is right. Moses says, “Come here; carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron's uncle Uzziel, come forward and do it just as Moses directed. I think this was a hard job to be handed.

Close on the words, but the direction is the opposite, friend. Moses tells Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron's uncle Uzziel, “carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” So the bodies go out of the camp, not into it. And they do exactly that.

Around is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word here. Moses tells Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron's uncle Uzziel, “carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” The word is outside, and they carry them out as Moses had directed. I think this was a hard job to be handed.

Yes, that's what Moses says. He tells Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair become disheveled and do not tear your garments, or else you will die…” (Leviticus 10:6). Eleazar and Ithamar are Aaron's two remaining sons. It's a serious instruction on a heavy day.

The text says the opposite, friend. Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair become disheveled and do not tear your garments, or else you will die…” So True is the answer, because they are told not to tear their garments. The verse goes on to say the LORD will be angry with the whole congregation.

You got it, baker. Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar to leave their hair alone and keep their garments untorn. But all of Israel is free to mourn over that fire. The priests stay at their post, and the people get to grieve. I think this was a heavy day for everybody.

Elders aren't mentioned in that verse, friend. Moses says, “But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn on account of the fire that the LORD has ignited.” That's the whole house of Israel, not a small group. Nobody gets left out of the mourning.

Not quite, friend. Moses is talking to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar when he says no messy hair and no torn garments. Then he turns to the whole house of Israel and says they may mourn. So grieving is allowed, and that instruction is only for Aaron and his sons.

Anointing is right. Moses tells Aaron and his sons not to go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, or they will die, “…for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you.” That oil marks them as set apart. And the text says they did as Moses instructed.

A lamp oil mix-up is easy to make, but that's not the oil in this verse. Moses says, “…for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you.” That's the reason Aaron and his sons must not go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. So the word we want is anointing.

Offerings are all over this chapter, so I see why that jumped out. But the verse says, “…for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you.” That oil is why Aaron and his sons must not go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, or they will die. The word is anointing.

Yes. The LORD tells Aaron, “You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come.” Listen to that last part: “…for the generations to come.” That's a rule with no expiration date, unlike the coupon I once shared a junk drawer with, which had one and believed in itself anyway.

The censers were part of the story earlier, so I see the connection. But that's not what the LORD says here. He tells Aaron, “You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die…” So the instruction is about wine and strong drink.

The text doesn't say anything about speaking to the people. The LORD tells Aaron, “You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come.” That's the instruction, and it lasts for the generations to come.

explanations.answer: So they can teach the Israelites His statutes
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says the priests must distinguish between the holy and the common, and the clean and the unclean, “…so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses.” So the priests have a teaching job. They have to know the difference in order to pass it on.

explanations.answer: So they can settle disputes between the tribes
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason the LORD gives, friend. He says the priests must know the holy from the common and the clean from the unclean “…so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses.” Settling disputes isn't mentioned. The reason is teaching.

explanations.answer: So they can count the people of each tribe
explanations.explanation: A head count sounds like a fine job for a priest, friend, but this verse doesn't give it as the reason. The LORD links knowing holy from common and clean from unclean to teaching the Israelites His statutes. You can't teach a recipe you don't know yourself. I'd be a terrible teacher if I couldn't tell dough from crumbs.

Angry is right. Moses went looking carefully for the goat of the sin offering and found it burned up. The text says he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. His next question shows what bothered him: why wasn't it eaten in the holy place, when it was given to take away the guilt of the congregation (Lev 10:17)?

Pleased would make for a quiet scene, but that's not what the text says. Moses finds the goat of the sin offering burned up, and “He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s remaining sons…” Then he asks them why they didn't eat it in the holy place. So the word is angry.

Moses does ask a question instead of just stating a verdict, so I see why patient came to mind. But the text says he “…was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s remaining sons…” That's the feeling the verse gives when he finds the goat burned up. So the word is angry.

Yes. Moses asks them, “Why didn’t you eat the sin offering in the holy place? For it is most holy; it was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD.” The sin offering had a big purpose. That's why he's asking so seriously.

explanations.answer: Thank the LORD for the harvest
explanations.explanation: Harvest thanks isn't in this verse, friend. Moses says the sin offering “…was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD.” So the offering is about guilt and atonement. That's why Moses asks the question the way he does.

explanations.answer: Mark the start of a new feast
explanations.explanation: A feast would be a happier reading, but the verse says something else. Moses tells Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, that the sin offering “…was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD.” So its job is taking away guilt through atonement. No feast is mentioned.

It's the other way around, friend. Moses says, “Since its blood was not brought inside the holy place, you should have eaten it in the sanctuary area, as I commanded.” So the blood was not brought inside, and that's why he says they should have eaten it. The correct answer is false.

Right. Moses says, “Since its blood was not brought inside the holy place, you should have eaten it in the sanctuary area, as I commanded.” He's talking to Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. The blood staying outside is the reason he gives for what they should have done.

explanations.answer: Would it have been acceptable to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Moses asked why the sin offering wasn't eaten in the holy place, and Aaron answers with a question of his own. He says that this very day they presented their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and that these things have happened to him. I think he means the loss of Nadab and Abihu. Then he asks whether eating the sin offering that day would have been acceptable in the LORD's sight.

explanations.answer: Was it his job or his sons' job
explanations.explanation: Whose job it was isn't what Aaron asks. He says, “…if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?” His question is about whether the LORD would accept it. He's talking to Moses, Israel's leader, and he's clear about it.

explanations.answer: Should it have been burned inside the camp
explanations.explanation: Burning inside the camp doesn't come up in Aaron's reply. He says, “…if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?” That's the question he puts to Moses, Israel's leader. It's about eating the offering that day.

Satisfied is right. Moses was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar when he found the goat burned up. Then he heard Aaron's explanation, and the text says he was satisfied. That's where the passage leaves Moses. I wish every kitchen argument could end with one honest answer like that.

Offended might seem likely after Moses was angry, but that's not what the text says. It says, “And when Moses heard this explanation, he was satisfied.” So Aaron's answer settled it. The word is satisfied.

Confused is a fair guess, since Aaron's answer is short and packed. But the text says, “And when Moses heard this explanation, he was satisfied.” Moses understood it and was content with it. The word is satisfied.
